title: Διήγησις καὶ ἐπιταγαί
titleEn: The Night’s Telling and the Morning Charge — Odyssey 23.288–372
part: The Night’s Telling and the Morning Charge (23.288–372)
about: With the bed made up by torchlight, Odysseus and Penelope go to it gladly, while Telemachus and the two herdsmen stop the dance and the household settles to sleep. The pair take their fill of love and then of talk: she tells all she endured in the halls from the suitors, and he tells his whole wandering, from the Cicones and the Lotus-eaters to Calypso and the Phaeacians, until sleep falls on him. Athena then sends Dawn up from Oceanus. Odysseus rises and charges his wife: they have both had their fill of trials; the flocks the suitors ate will be made good; he will go to his father's farm, and she is to go up to her room with her women and speak to no one, since word of the dead suitors will spread with the sun. He arms himself, rouses his son and the herdsmen, and they go out armed, with Athena hiding them in night while the light spreads over the earth.

sentences.t: ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον·
sentences.l: So they, such things to one another were saying;
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another;
sentences.n: Read οἱ μὲν as ‘they’: in Homer the ‘article’ is a pronoun, and μέν waits for the δέ of τόφρα δ’ in the next line, which sets the pair who have been talking against the women preparing the bed. τοιαῦτα is ‘such things’, the object of ἀγόρευον, the unaugmented imperfect of ἀγορεύω ‘speak aloud’. πρὸς ἀλλήλους is ‘to one another’. The pair are Odysseus and Penelope, as οἱ μὲν ἔπειτα in 295–296 shows. This line stands word for word elsewhere in the poem, where it closes a different scene.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δ’ ἄρ’ Εὐρυνόμη τε ἰδὲ τροφὸς ἔντυον εὐνὴν
ἐσθῆτος μαλακῆς, δαΐδων ὕπο λαμπομενάων.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile then Eurynome and the nurse were making ready the couch
of soft bedding, under blazing torches.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Eurynome and the nurse made the couch ready with soft coverings, by the light of blazing torches.
sentences.n: τόφρα means ‘meanwhile’. τε … ἰδέ is ‘both … and’ (ἰδέ is epic for ἠδέ), joining Εὐρυνόμη and τροφός, the nurse. ἔντυον is the unaugmented imperfect of ἐντύω ‘make ready’. ἐσθῆτος μαλακῆς is a genitive of material, ‘of soft bedding’ (ἐσθής is any covering or clothing). δαΐδων ὕπο: ὕπο stands after its noun with its accent drawn back, and with the genitive gives the circumstance, ‘under torches’. λαμπομενάων is the genitive plural participle of λάμπομαι ‘shine, blaze’, with the epic ending -άων (Attic -ων).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ στόρεσαν πυκινὸν λέχος ἐγκονέουσαι,
γρηῢς μὲν κείουσα πάλιν οἶκόνδε βεβήκει,
τοῖσιν δ’ Εὐρυνόμη θαλαμηπόλος ἡγεμόνευεν
ἐρχομένοισι λέχοσδε, δάος μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχουσα·
sentences.l:
But when they had spread the solid bed, bustling about,
the old woman, wishing to lie down, back homeward had gone,
and for them Eurynome, the chamber-attendant, was leading the way,
as they went to the bed, holding a torch in her hands;
sentences.i: But when they had made up the solid bed, working with speed, the old woman, wanting to lie down, went back to the house, and Eurynome, the chamber-attendant, led the way for the two of them as they went to the bed, holding a torch in her hands.
sentences.n: γρηῢς is ‘old woman’ (Attic γραῦς), the nurse of 289; κείουσα is the participle of κείω, a form of κεῖμαι ‘lie’ that means ‘wishing to lie down’, and βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had gone’, used here for a plain past. μὲν in 292 is answered by δέ in τοῖσιν δ’ in 293. τοῖσιν is a pronoun, ‘for them’ (the pair), and ἐρχομένοισι agrees with it: ‘for them as they went’. θαλαμηπόλος is ‘chamber-attendant’, and Εὐρυνόμη is her name in apposition. λέχοσδε is λέχος ‘bed’ with the suffix -δε (here -σδε) of motion towards: ‘to the bed’. The sentence runs four lines, and ends at the ano teleia. 291 is a line that stands word for word elsewhere in the poem, and keeps its English.

sentences.t: ἐς θάλαμον δ’ ἀγαγοῦσα πάλιν κίεν.
sentences.l: and into the chamber having led them, back she went.
sentences.i: and when she had led them into the chamber, she went back.
sentences.n: Eurynome is still the subject. ἀγαγοῦσα is the aorist participle of ἄγω ‘lead’, feminine, and ‘them’ is understood from the dative pair of 293. κίεν is the unaugmented imperfect of κίω ‘go’, here ‘she went’, with πάλιν ‘back’. The sentence ends in the middle of the line, after κίεν; οἱ μὲν ἔπειτα, ‘they then’, begins the next unit.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἔπειτα
ἀσπάσιοι λέκτροιο παλαιοῦ θεσμὸν ἵκοντο·
sentences.l:
They then
glad the ordinance of the old bed reached;
sentences.i: And they, glad, then came to the ancient ordinance of their bed.
sentences.n: οἱ μὲν is ‘they’ again, now the pair themselves. ἀσπάσιοι is the adjective ‘glad’ in the nominative plural. θεσμόν, from τίθημι, is ‘what is laid down, an ordinance’; it is a rare word and its force here (the settled rite of the marriage bed, or the old arrangement of their life together) is not certain, so the English keeps the word ‘ordinance’. λέκτροιο παλαιοῦ is a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου): ‘of the old bed’. ἵκοντο is the unaugmented aorist middle of ἵκω ‘come to’, with the accusative θεσμόν.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Τηλέμαχος καὶ βουκόλος ἠδὲ συβώτης
παῦσαν ἄρ’ ὀρχηθμοῖο πόδας, παῦσαν δὲ γυναῖκας,
αὐτοὶ δ’ εὐνάζοντο κατὰ μέγαρα σκιόεντα.
sentences.l:
But Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd
stopped then from the dance the feet, and stopped the women,
and themselves went to sleep throughout the shadowy halls.
sentences.i: Telemachus, the cowherd and the swineherd stopped the feet from dancing, and stopped the women too, and went to sleep themselves throughout the shadowy halls.
sentences.n: The three men named in 297 are the subject of the two verbs both called παῦσαν, the unaugmented aorist of παύω ‘make cease’ (the repetition is emphatic), and αὐτοί picks them up again for a third verb. ὀρχηθμοῖο is a genitive in -οιο of separation: they made the feet cease ‘from the dance’. Whose feet is not said: the men’s own and the women’s are both in view, and the second παῦσαν adds the women. αὐτοί is ‘themselves’; εὐνάζοντο is the imperfect middle of εὐνάζω ‘lay to rest’, ‘were going to sleep’. κατὰ μέγαρα σκιόεντα is ‘through the shadowy halls’. Line 297 stands word for word elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν φιλότητος ἐταρπήτην ἐρατεινῆς,
τερπέσθην μύθοισι, πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἐνέποντε,
sentences.l:
And those two, when then they had had their fill of lovely love,
enjoyed themselves in words, to one another telling,
sentences.i: When those two had taken their fill of lovely love, they took pleasure in words, speaking to one another,
sentences.n: τὼ is the dual of the pronoun, ‘those two’, Odysseus and Penelope. The Greek keeps the dual through the passage: ἐταρπήτην and τερπέσθην are dual verbs and ἐνέποντε is a dual participle, so read ‘the pair of them’ throughout. ἐταρπήτην is from τέρπω in the passive sense ‘take one’s fill of’, with the genitive φιλότητος; ἐρατεινῆς ‘lovely’ is the genitive feminine. οὖν is ‘then’. The unit stops at a comma, because the sentence it begins would run six lines.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ὅσ’ ἐν μεγάροισιν ἀνέσχετο δῖα γυναικῶν,
ἀνδρῶν μνηστήρων ἐσορῶσ’ ἀΐδηλον ὅμιλον,
οἳ ἕθεν εἵνεκα πολλά, βόας καὶ ἴφια μῆλα,
ἔσφαζον, πολλὸς δὲ πίθων ἠφύσσετο οἶνος·
sentences.l:
She, how much she endured in the halls, heavenly-one of women,
looking upon the ruinous throng of men, the suitors,
who for her sake many things, cattle and stout flocks,
were slaughtering, and much wine was drawn from the jars;
sentences.i: She told how much she had endured in the halls, heavenly among women, as she looked on at the ruinous throng of the suitors, who for her sake slaughtered so many cattle and stout flocks, while great quantities of wine were drawn from the jars;
sentences.n: ἡ μὲν is ‘she’, set against αὐτὰρ ὁ ‘but he’ in 306; the verb of telling is carried over from ἐνέποντε in the line before, so ὅσ’ ἀνέσχετο is ‘how much she endured’. δῖα γυναικῶν is Penelope’s stock epithet: ‘heavenly among women’. ἀΐδηλον is a word of disputed sense, either ‘destroying, ruinous’ or ‘unseen, hidden’; we keep ‘ruinous’. ἐσορῶσ’ is the participle ‘looking at’. In οἳ ἕθεν εἵνεκα, ἕθεν is the pronoun ‘her’ and εἵνεκα (= ἕνεκα) follows it: ‘for her sake’. ἴφια μῆλα is ‘stout flocks’. ἔσφαζον is the imperfect of σφάζω ‘slaughter’; πίθων is the genitive of πίθος ‘wine-jar’, the source of the drawing; ἠφύσσετο is the passive imperfect of ἀφύσσω ‘draw’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ διογενὴς Ὀδυσεὺς ὅσα κήδε’ ἔθηκεν
ἀνθρώποις ὅσα τ’ αὐτὸς ὀϊζύσας ἐμόγησε,
πάντ’ ἔλεγ’·
sentences.i: And he, Zeus-born Odysseus, told all the sorrows he had brought upon men and all that he himself had toiled through in distress;
sentences.n: διογενής is ‘Zeus-sprung’, the stock epithet of Odysseus. The sentence is built on two clauses of quantity, ὅσα … ὅσα τε ‘all that … and all that’, both resumed by πάντ’, which is the object of ἔλεγ’ (the imperfect of λέγω, ‘was telling’). κήδεα ἔθηκεν is ‘set sorrows’ upon people, that is, caused them; ἀνθρώποις is the dative of those who received them. ὀϊζύσας is the aorist participle of ὀϊζύω ‘suffer distress’, and ἐμόγησε the aorist of μογέω ‘toil’. The unit ends in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐτέρπετ’ ἀκούουσ’, οὐδέ οἱ ὕπνος
πῖπτεν ἐπὶ βλεφάροισι πάρος καταλέξαι ἅπαντα.
sentences.l:
and she then was delighting, listening, and not for her sleep
fell upon her eyelids before he had recounted everything.
sentences.i: and she listened with delight, and sleep did not fall upon her eyelids until he had told her everything.
sentences.n: ἐτέρπετ’ is the elided imperfect middle of τέρπω, ‘was delighting’, with ἀκούουσ’ ‘listening’. οὐδέ οἱ ὕπνος: οἱ is the dative pronoun ‘to her’, not a nominative, so the phrase is ‘nor to her sleep’. πάρος with an infinitive means ‘before’ (Attic πρίν), and καταλέξαι is the aorist infinitive of καταλέγω ‘recount’, whose subject ‘he’ is left to the context; ἅπαντα is its object. βλεφάροισι is a dative plural in -οισι.

sentences.t:
ἤρξατο δ’ ὡς πρῶτον Κίκονας δάμασ’, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
ἦλθ’ ἐς Λωτοφάγων ἀνδρῶν πίειραν ἄρουραν·
sentences.l:
He began how first the Cicones he overcame, and then
he went to the rich plough-land of the Lotus-eating men;
sentences.i: He began with how he first overcame the Cicones, and then came to the rich land of the Lotus-eaters;
sentences.n: From here to 341 the poet summarises the tale in a run of clauses, most of them opening ἠδ’ ὡς or ὥς θ’, ‘and how’ (ἠδέ is the epic ‘and’), each a summary of what Odysseus told. Here the first is ἤρξατο δ’ ὡς: ‘he began how’; ἤρξατο is the aorist middle of ἄρχω ‘begin’. δάμασ’ is the aorist of δαμάζω ‘overpower’, unaugmented. αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα is ‘and then’; αὐτάρ in this use is not ‘but’. ἦλθ’ is the aorist of ἔρχομαι. Λωτοφάγων is ‘of the Lotus-eaters’, ἀνδρῶν ‘men’ in apposition; πίειραν is ‘rich’ (fat, fertile), agreeing with ἄρουραν ‘plough-land’.

sentences.t:
ἠδ’ ὅσα Κύκλωψ ἔρξε, καὶ ὡς ἀπετίσατο ποινὴν
ἰφθίμων ἑτάρων, οὓς ἤσθιεν οὐδ’ ἐλέαιρεν·
sentences.l:
and all the Cyclops did, and how he exacted payment
for his mighty companions, whom he ate and did not pity;
sentences.i: and all that the Cyclops did, and how he exacted payment for his mighty companions, whom the Cyclops ate without pity;
sentences.n: ὅσα Κύκλωψ ἔρξε is ‘all that the Cyclops did’, ἔρξε being the aorist of ἔρδω ‘do’. ἀπετίσατο is the aorist middle of ἀποτίνω, whose middle means ‘exact a penalty’; ποινήν is the penalty, and ἰφθίμων ἑτάρων, the genitive of the thing paid for, ‘for his mighty companions’. ἰφθίμων is ‘mighty, stout’. οὓς is the relative, ‘whom’; the Cyclops is the subject of ἤσθιεν ‘was eating’ and ἐλέαιρεν ‘pitied’.

sentences.t:
ἠδ’ ὡς Αἴολον ἵκεθ’, ὅ μιν πρόφρων ὑπέδεκτο
καὶ πέμπ’, οὐδέ πω αἶσα φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ ἱκέσθαι
ἤην, ἀλλά μιν αὖτις ἀναρπάξασα θύελλα
πόντον ἐπ’ ἰχθυόεντα φέρεν βαρέα στενάχοντα·
sentences.l:
and how he came to Aeolus, who ready-minded received him
and was sending him on; nor yet was destiny, to his dear fatherland to come,
there for him, but again a storm-blast, snatching him up,
bore him, groaning heavily, over the fish-teeming sea;
sentences.i: and how he came to Aeolus, who received him with a ready mind and sent him on his way; it was not yet his destined portion to reach his dear fatherland, but a storm-blast caught him up again and carried him off, groaning heavily, across the fish-teeming sea;
sentences.n: ὅ here is best taken as the relative ‘who’ (the accent is the one it takes before the enclitic μιν, and ‘he’ would also fit the grammar): it heads the clause ὅ μιν πρόφρων ὑπέδεκτο, ‘who received him readily’ (πρόφρων ‘ready-minded’; ὑπέδεκτο is the aorist middle of ὑποδέχομαι). πέμπ’ is πέμπε, the unaugmented imperfect of πέμπω ‘send’, with καί joining it to ὑπέδεκτο. αἶσα is ‘portion, destiny’; ἤην is the epic imperfect ‘was’ (Attic ἦν), and ἱκέσθαι ‘to reach’ depends on αἶσα. θύελλα is the ‘storm-blast’; ἀναρπάξασα is its aorist participle ‘snatching up’, and βαρέα στενάχοντα, accusative with μιν, means that it is Odysseus who groans. The last two lines stand in part elsewhere in the poem, and the English follows that wording.

sentences.t:
ἠδ’ ὡς Τηλέπυλον Λαιστρυγονίην ἀφίκανεν,
οἳ νῆάς τ’ ὄλεσαν καὶ ἐϋκνήμιδας ἑταίρους
πάντας·
sentences.i: and how he came to Laestrygonian Telepylus, whose people destroyed his ships and all his well-greaved companions;
sentences.n: Λαιστρυγονίην is an adjective, ‘Laestrygonian’, agreeing with Τηλέπυλον, the city. ἀφίκανεν is a lengthened form of ἀφικνέομαι ‘arrive at’. οἳ is the relative plural: the Laestrygonians, the people of the city. ὄλεσαν is the unaugmented aorist of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’. ἐϋκνήμιδας is ‘well-greaved’, fitted with shin-guards (κνημῖδες), the stock epithet of companions; πάντας ‘all’ belongs with ἑταίρους and ends the sentence at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: Ὀδυσσεὺς δ’ οἶος ὑπέκφυγε νηῒ μελαίνῃ·
sentences.l: but Odysseus alone escaped with a black ship;
sentences.i: but Odysseus alone got clear away in a black ship;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of the line. οἶος is the epic ‘alone’ (Attic μόνος). ὑπέκφυγε is the aorist of ὑπεκφεύγω ‘escape from under’, with the preverbs ὑπό and ἐκ and no augment. νηῒ μελαίνῃ is a dative of means or accompaniment: ‘with a black ship’.

sentences.t: καὶ Κίρκης κατέλεξε δόλον πολυμηχανίην τε,
sentences.l: and of Circe he recounted the guile and the many-devising craft too,
sentences.i: and he told of Circe’s guile and her many devices,
sentences.n: Κίρκης is a genitive depending on both nouns: the guile of Circe and her many-devising craft. κατέλεξε is the aorist of καταλέγω ‘recount’ (compare καταλέξαι in 309). δόλον is ‘guile, trick’; πολυμηχανίην, built on πολύ and μηχανή ‘device’, is the abstract noun beside the adjective πολυμήχανος ‘man of many devices’. The unit stops at a comma, because the sentence it begins would run five lines.

sentences.t:
ἠδ’ ὡς εἰς Ἀΐδεω δόμον ἤλυθεν εὐρώεντα,
ψυχῇ χρησόμενος Θηβαίου Τειρεσίαο,
νηῒ πολυκλήϊδι, καὶ εἴσιδε πάντας ἑταίρους
μητέρα θ’, ἥ μιν ἔτικτε καὶ ἔτρεφε τυτθὸν ἐόντα·
sentences.l:
and how to the house of Hades he went, the mouldy one,
to consult the soul of Theban Teiresias,
in a many-thwarted ship, and saw all his companions
and his mother, who bore him and nurtured him when he was little;
sentences.i: and how he went to the dank house of Hades to consult the soul of Theban Teiresias, in his many-thwarted ship, and saw all his companions and his mother, who bore him and brought him up when he was small;
sentences.n: Ἀΐδεω is the Ionic genitive of Hades (Attic Ἅιδου), and εὐρώεντα ‘mouldy, dank’ agrees with δόμον ‘house’. χρησόμενος is the future participle of χράομαι, whose dative ψυχῇ (the soul of Teiresias) gives ‘to consult’: the future participle expresses purpose. Θηβαίου is ‘Theban’. In νηῒ πολυκλήϊδι the adjective comes from κληΐς, a fitting of a ship’s rowing; whether thwarts, benches or oar-fastenings is not certain, and ‘many-thwarted’ is the traditional gloss. εἴσιδε is the aorist of εἰσοράω ‘catch sight of’, with two objects, πάντας ἑταίρους and μητέρα. ἥ is the relative ‘who’, μιν ‘him’, and τυτθὸν ἐόντα is ‘being little’ (ἐόντα is the epic participle of εἰμί, Attic ὄντα).

sentences.t:
ἠδ’ ὡς Σειρήνων ἁδινάων φθόγγον ἄκουσεν,
ὥς θ’ ἵκετο Πλαγκτὰς πέτρας δεινήν τε Χάρυβδιν
Σκύλλην θ’, ἣν οὔ πώ ποτ’ ἀκήριοι ἄνδρες ἄλυξαν·
sentences.i: and how he heard the voice of the thronging Sirens, and how he came to the Wandering Rocks and dread Charybdis and Scylla, whom no men have ever yet escaped uninjured;
sentences.n: ἁδινάων is a genitive plural feminine in -άων agreeing with Σειρήνων, not with φθόγγον: ‘of the thronging Sirens’. ἁδινός means ‘thick, close-packed’; said of a voice or of the Sirens, its sense is not certain (some take it as ‘clear’ or ‘shrill’), and ‘thronging’ keeps the one word used elsewhere. ὥς θ’ is ὡς τε, ‘and how’. Πλαγκτάς is the adjective ‘wandering’ (related to πλάζω ‘drive astray’), agreeing with πέτρας ‘rocks’. δεινήν is ‘dread’; Σκύλλην θ’ adds a third object of ἵκετο. ἀκήριοι is ‘uninjured’, and ἄλυξαν the aorist of ἀλύσκω ‘escape’.

sentences.t: ἠδ’ ὡς Ἠελίοιο βόας κατέπεφνον ἑταῖροι·
sentences.l: and how of the Sun the cattle killed the companions;
sentences.i: and how his companions killed the cattle of the Sun;
sentences.n: Ἠελίοιο is the Ionic genitive of the Sun (Attic Ἡλίου), and βόας the accusative plural of βοῦς ‘cow, ox’, the object of κατέπεφνον. κατέπεφνον is an aorist of the root φεν- ‘strike, kill’, with a reduplicated stem and the preverb κατά; the subject ἑταῖροι stands last, in the nominative.

sentences.t:
ἠδ’ ὡς νῆα θοὴν ἔβαλε ψολόεντι κεραυνῷ
Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης, ἀπὸ δ’ ἔφθιθεν ἐσθλοὶ ἑταῖροι
πάντες ὁμῶς, αὐτὸς δὲ κακὰς ὑπὸ κῆρας ἄλυξεν·
sentences.i: and how Zeus, who thunders on high, struck the swift ship with a smoky thunderbolt, and all his good companions perished together, but he himself escaped the evil fates of death;
sentences.n: ἔβαλε is the aorist of βάλλω ‘strike’, with the instrumental dative ψολόεντι κεραυνῷ ‘with a smoky thunderbolt’ (ψολόεις is from ψόλος ‘soot’). ὑψιβρεμέτης, from ὑψι- ‘on high’ and βρέμω ‘roar’, is the epithet of Zeus: ‘high-thundering’. ἀπὸ δ’ ἔφθιθεν is tmesis: ἀπό belongs with ἔφθιθεν, a third plural aorist of φθίνω, so the pair is ‘perished away’. ἐσθλοὶ ἑταῖροι is ‘good companions’. κακὰς ὑπὸ κῆρας ἄλυξεν is also tmesis, ὑπό with ἄλυξεν; κῆρες (plural of κήρ ‘death-fate’) is the object, a different word from κῆρ ‘heart’.

sentences.t:
ὥς θ’ ἵκετ’ Ὠγυγίην νῆσον νύμφην τε Καλυψώ,
ἣ δή μιν κατέρυκε, λιλαιομένη πόσιν εἶναι,
ἐν σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσι, καὶ ἔτρεφεν ἠδὲ ἔφασκε
θήσειν ἀθάνατον καὶ ἀγήραον ἤματα πάντα·
sentences.l:
and how he came to the Ogygian island and the nymph Calypso,
who indeed held him back, longing for him to be her husband,
in hollow caves, and nurtured him and kept saying
she would make him immortal and ageless all his days;
sentences.i: and how he came to the Ogygian island and the nymph Calypso, who kept him there, wanting him for her husband, in her hollow caves, and nurtured him, and kept telling him she would make him immortal and ageless for all his days;
sentences.n: Ὠγυγίην is an adjective, ‘Ogygian’, agreeing with νῆσον. ἣ is the relative ‘who’. κατέρυκε is the imperfect of κατερύκω ‘hold back, detain’; λιλαιομένη πόσιν εἶναι is ‘longing for him to be her husband’ (the participle of λιλαίομαι with an infinitive; ‘him’ is understood). ἐν σπέσσι γλαφυροῖσι has the dative plural in -εσσι of σπέος ‘cave’. ἔτρεφεν is ‘nurtured’, and ἔφασκε is an iterative imperfect (suffix -σκ-) of φημί, ‘kept saying’. θήσειν is the future infinitive of τίθημι, ‘would make’; ἀγήραον is ‘ageless’ (a- + γῆρας), and ἤματα πάντα an accusative of time, ‘all his days’. The last line stands word for word elsewhere in the poem, and keeps its English.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τοῦ οὔ ποτε θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἔπειθεν·
sentences.l: but of him never the heart within his breast did she persuade;
sentences.i: but she never persuaded his heart within his breast;
sentences.n: τοῦ is a genitive pronoun that belongs with θυμόν, and means ‘his’, the heart of him. ἔπειθεν is an imperfect with the sense of persistent effort that fails: ‘she kept trying to persuade, and never did’. ἐνὶ is ἐν, and στήθεσσιν a dative plural in -εσσι. οὔ ποτε is ‘never’. ἀλλά opens the contrast with the promise before it.

sentences.t:
ἠδ’ ὡς ἐς Φαίηκας ἀφίκετο πολλὰ μογήσας,
οἳ δή μιν περὶ κῆρι θεὸν ὣς τιμήσαντο
καὶ πέμψαν σὺν νηῒ φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν,
χαλκόν τε χρυσόν τε ἅλις ἐσθῆτά τε δόντες.
sentences.l:
and how to the Phaeacians he came, having toiled much,
who indeed honored him in their hearts as a god
and sent him with a ship to his dear fatherland,
bronze and gold in abundance, and clothing, giving,
sentences.i: and how he came to the Phaeacians, after much toil, who honored him in their hearts like a god and sent him with a ship to his dear fatherland, giving him bronze and gold in plenty, and clothing.
sentences.n: πολλὰ μογήσας is ‘having toiled much’, the aorist participle of μογέω with πολλά as an adverb. οἳ δή begins the relative clause ‘who indeed’, about the Phaeacians. περὶ κῆρι: περί is adverbial and strengthens ‘in their hearts’; the English follows the wording already given to this line elsewhere in the poem. θεὸν ὣς is ‘like a god’, with ὥς after its noun. πέμψαν is the unaugmented aorist of πέμπω. The last line, χαλκόν τε χρυσόν τε ἅλις ἐσθῆτά τε δόντες, stands word for word elsewhere in the poem, and keeps its English; ἅλις is ‘in abundance’, and δόντες is the aorist participle of δίδωμι.

sentences.t:
τοῦτ’ ἄρα δεύτατον εἶπεν ἔπος, ὅτε οἱ γλυκὺς ὕπνος
λυσιμελὴς ἐπόρουσε, λύων μελεδήματα θυμοῦ.
sentences.l:
This then last word he said, when on him sweet sleep,
limb-loosening, rushed, loosing the cares of his heart.
sentences.i: This was the last word he spoke, when sweet sleep came upon him, slackening his limbs and loosing the cares of his heart.
sentences.n: τοῦτο … ἔπος is ‘this word’, with δεύτατον ‘last’ (the epic superlative of δεύτερος) as its predicate. ὅτε οἱ is ‘when on him’: οἱ is the dative pronoun. ἐπόρουσε is the aorist of ἐπόρνυμι ‘rush upon’, with ὕπνος as subject. λυσιμελής is ‘limb-loosening’ (λύω and μέλος ‘limb’), and λύων … μελεδήματα θυμοῦ ‘loosing the cares of his heart’ is a participle phrase agreeing with ὕπνος.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: And she again another thing devised, the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena;
sentences.i: And in her turn the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, thought of something else:
sentences.n: ἡ is the pronoun ‘she’. αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn, again’, and ἄλλ’ is ἄλλα ‘another thing’, the object of ἐνόησε, the aorist of νοέω ‘devise’; ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε sets the goddess’s own thought against what Odysseus and Penelope have been doing. θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη is ‘the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena’; the sense of γλαυκῶπις, ‘gleaming’ or ‘grey’ eyed, is old and disputed.

sentences.t:
ὁππότε δή ῥ’ Ὀδυσῆα ἐέλπετο ὃν κατὰ θυμὸν
εὐνῆς ἧς ἀλόχου ταρπήμεναι ἠδὲ καὶ ὕπνου,
αὐτίκ’ ἀπ’ Ὠκεανοῦ χρυσόθρονον ἠριγένειαν
ὦρσεν, ἵν’ ἀνθρώποισι φόως φέροι·
sentences.l:
when indeed Odysseus she supposed, in her own heart,
to have taken his fill of the couch of his own wife and of sleep too,
at once from Oceanus golden-throned early-born Dawn
she roused, that for men light she might bring;
sentences.i: As soon as she judged in her own heart that Odysseus had taken his fill of the couch of his own wife and of sleep, she at once roused golden-throned, early-born Dawn from Oceanus, to bring light to men;
sentences.n: ὁππότε is ‘when’ (Attic ὁπότε). ὃν κατὰ θυμόν is ‘in her own heart’, and ἧς in εὐνῆς ἧς ἀλόχου is ‘his own’: ὅς, ἥ, ὅν is the possessive adjective ‘one’s own’, easily mistaken for the relative. ἐέλπετο is the imperfect of ἔλπομαι ‘expect, suppose’. ταρπήμεναι is the aorist passive infinitive of τέρπω (Attic ταρπῆναι), ‘to have had his fill’, with genitives. ἠριγένειαν ‘early-born’ and χρυσόθρονον ‘golden-throned’ name Dawn by her two epithets alone, without Ἠώς; an old alternative derives the second part of χρυσόθρονος from θρόνα ‘flowers’, not ‘thrones’. ὦρσεν is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’. ἵν’ … φέροι is a purpose clause with the optative. The unit ends in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ὦρτο δ’ Ὀδυσσεὺς
εὐνῆς ἐκ μαλακῆς, ἀλόχῳ δ’ ἐπὶ μῦθον ἔτελλεν·
sentences.l:
and rose Odysseus
from the soft couch, and upon his wife a word he laid as charge:
sentences.i: and Odysseus rose from the soft couch and laid his charge on his wife with these words:
sentences.n: ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι, ‘he rose’, the same verb in the active as ὦρσεν in the line before (‘she roused’). εὐνῆς ἐκ μαλακῆς is ‘out of the soft couch’. ἐπὶ … ἔτελλεν is tmesis for ἐπιτέλλω ‘lay a charge upon’, with the dative ἀλόχῳ ‘wife’ and the accusative μῦθον, here ‘instruction’. The charge that follows is the speech, which runs to 365 and is Odysseus’ instructions to Penelope.

sentences.t:
ὦ γύναι, ἤδη μὲν πολέων κεκορήμεθ’ ἀέθλων
ἀμφοτέρω, σὺ μὲν ἐνθάδ’ ἐμὸν πολυκηδέα νόστον
κλαίουσ’.
sentences.l:
“O wife, already of many trials we have had our fill,
we two, you here my many-sorrowed homecoming
weeping.
sentences.i: “Wife, we two have already had our fill of many trials — you here, weeping over my homecoming, so full of sorrows.
sentences.n: ὦ γύναι is ‘O wife’, the vocative of γυνή. κεκορήμεθ’ is the perfect passive of κορέννυμι ‘satisfy’, ‘we have been satisfied’, with the genitive πολέων ἀέθλων, ‘of many trials’. ἀμφοτέρω is the dual, ‘both of us’, taken with the plural verb. σὺ μὲν awaits its αὐτὰρ ἐμέ in the next unit: ‘you here … but me …’. κλαίουσ’ is the participle ‘weeping’, agreeing with σύ and governing νόστον. πολυκηδέα is ‘many-sorrowed’, from πολύ and κῆδος ‘sorrow, care’. The sentence ends in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμὲ Ζεὺς ἄλγεσι καὶ θεοὶ ἄλλοι
ἱέμενον πεδάασκον ἐμῆς ἀπὸ πατρίδος αἴης·
sentences.l:
but me Zeus with pains and the other gods
eager kept binding fast, away from my fatherland;
sentences.i: But as for me, Zeus and the other gods kept binding me with pains, eager as I was, away from my own fatherland;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of the line. ἐμέ is the object ‘me’, placed first against σύ. ἱέμενον agrees with ἐμέ: ‘though I was eager’, the eagerness being to return, as in 1.6 ἱέμενός περ. πεδάασκον is an iterative imperfect (suffix -σκ-) of πεδάω ‘bind, hold fast’: ‘kept binding’. ἄλγεσι is a dative of means. ἀπό stands between ἐμῆς and πατρίδος, ‘away from my fatherland’, in ἐμῆς ἀπὸ πατρίδος αἴης; αἴης is a poetic word for ‘land’ with the Ionic η.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἐπεὶ ἀμφοτέρω πολυήρατον ἱκόμεθ’ εὐνήν,
κτήματα μὲν τά μοι ἔστι, κομιζέμεν ἐν μεγάροισι,
sentences.l:
But now, since we two to the much-loved couch have come,
the possessions that are mine, to look after in the halls,
sentences.i: But now that we two have come to our beloved couch, you are to look after the possessions that are mine in the halls,
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ἐπεὶ begins the sentence: ‘but now, since …’. ἱκόμεθ’ is the aorist middle of ἱκνέομαι ‘come to’. πολυήρατον is ‘much-loved, beloved’, from ἔρατος. κτήματα μὲν τά μοι ἔστι is ‘the possessions that are mine’, and κομιζέμεν is an active infinitive standing for an order, with κτήματα as its object: ‘look after the possessions’. The person ordered, Penelope, is left to be supplied, and the English writes ‘you’. μέν is answered by δέ at μῆλα δ’ in the next unit. The unit stops at a comma, because the sentence would run five lines.

sentences.t:
μῆλα δ’ ἅ μοι μνηστῆρες ὑπερφίαλοι κατέκειραν,
πολλὰ μὲν αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ληΐσσομαι, ἄλλα δ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
δώσουσ’, εἰς ὅ κε πάντας ἐνιπλήσωσιν ἐπαύλους.
sentences.l:
but the flocks that to me the overweening suitors shore down,
many I myself shall carry off as booty, and others the Achaeans
will give, until they fill all the folds.
sentences.i: As for the flocks of mine that the overweening suitors consumed, I shall carry off many as booty myself, and the Achaeans will give others, until they have filled all the folds.
sentences.n: μῆλα are ‘flocks’, the object of the relative clause ἅ μοι … κατέκειραν, ‘which to me … shore down’: κατακείρω ‘shear off’ is used of eating a property away, and μοι is a dative of loss. ὑπερφίαλοι is ‘overweening’. πολλὰ μὲν … ἄλλα δ’ is ‘many … and others’. ληΐσσομαι is the future middle of ληΐζομαι ‘carry off as booty’, and δώσουσ’ the future of δίδωμι. εἰς ὅ κε … ἐνιπλήσωσιν is ‘until they fill’, with κε and the aorist subjunctive; ἐπαύλους are the folds or steadings where the flocks stand.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι μὲν ἐγὼ πολυδένδρεον ἀγρὸν ἔπειμι,
ὀψόμενος πατέρ’ ἐσθλόν, ὅ μοι πυκινῶς ἀκάχηται·
sentences.l:
But truly I, for my part, to the farm rich in trees will go,
to see my good father, who for me is closely grieved;
sentences.i: But for my part, I shall go to the farm rich in trees, to see my good father, who is deeply grieved on my account;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι μὲν ἐγώ is ‘but truly I, for my part’, with the μέν waiting for σοὶ δέ in the next unit. ἔπειμι is ἐπί + εἶμι, ‘I shall go to’; the present of εἶμι carries the sense of the future. πολυδένδρεον is ‘rich in trees’ (πολύ and δένδρον). ὀψόμενος is the future participle of ὁράω, expressing purpose. ὅ is taken as the relative ‘who’ (accented before the enclitic μοι), and ἀκάχηται the perfect middle of ἀκαχίζω ‘distress’, ‘is grieved’; μοι is the person on whose account, and πυκινῶς ‘closely, deeply’.

sentences.t: σοὶ δέ, γύναι, τάδ’ ἐπιτέλλω, πινυτῇ περ ἐούσῃ·
sentences.l: but to you, wife, these things I charge, discerning though you are;
sentences.i: But to you, wife, I give this charge, discerning though you are.
sentences.n: σοί is ‘to you’, with τάδε ‘these things’ the object of ἐπιτέλλω, the same verb that stood in tmesis at 349. πινυτῇ ἐούσῃ is a dative participle phrase agreeing with σοί, and περ gives it concessive force: ‘though you are discerning’. ἐούσῃ is the epic participle of εἰμί (Attic οὔσῃ). γύναι is ‘wife’ again.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα γὰρ φάτις εἶσιν ἅμ’ ἠελίῳ ἀνιόντι
ἀνδρῶν μνηστήρων, οὓς ἔκτανον ἐν μεγάροισιν·
sentences.l:
For at once a rumour will go with the sun as it rises
of the men, the suitors, whom I killed in the halls;
sentences.i: For at once, with the rising of the sun, a rumour will go abroad about the men, the suitors, whom I killed in the halls;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for the charge: speed is needed, because the news will travel. φάτις is ‘report, rumour’, from φημί, and εἶσιν is the present of εἶμι with the sense of the future, ‘will go’. ἅμ’ ἠελίῳ ἀνιόντι is ‘with the sun as it rises’, with the Ionic dative ἠελίῳ and the participle ἀνιόντι of ἄνειμι. ἀνδρῶν μνηστήρων is a genitive depending on φάτις, ‘of the men, the suitors’, and οὓς is the relative ‘whom’. ἔκτανον is the aorist of κτείνω.

sentences.t:
εἰς ὑπερῷ’ ἀναβᾶσα σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξὶν
ἧσθαι, μηδέ τινα προτιόσσεο μηδ’ ἐρέεινε.
sentences.l:
having gone up to the upper chamber with your attendant women,
to sit; and do not look at anyone, nor question anyone.”
sentences.i: go up to your upper room with your attendant women and sit there, and do not look at anyone or ask anyone questions.”
sentences.n: Read ἀναβᾶσα, the feminine aorist participle of ἀναβαίνω, with ἧσθαι: ‘having gone up … sit’, so ‘go up … and sit’. ἧσθαι is the infinitive of ἧμαι ‘sit’, standing for an order as κομιζέμεν did at 355. ὑπερῷ’ is ὑπερῷα, ‘upper rooms’, and ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξίν is ‘attendant women’ (dative). μηδέ … μηδ’ is ‘nor … nor’, with two imperatives: προτιόσσεο, middle of the rare προτιόσσομαι ‘look toward, regard’, and ἐρέεινε, active, ‘question’. The line 364 stands word for word elsewhere in the poem, and keeps its English. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισιν ἐδύσετο τεύχεα καλά,
ὦρσε δὲ Τηλέμαχον καὶ βουκόλον ἠδὲ συβώτην,
πάντας δ’ ἔντε’ ἄνωγεν ἀρήϊα χερσὶν ἑλέσθαι.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and around his shoulders put on his fine armour,
and roused Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd,
and bade them all take warlike gear in their hands.
sentences.i: So he said, and put his fine armour about his shoulders, and roused Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd, and bade them all to take warlike gear in their hands.
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί is the narrator’s ‘he spoke, and’, closing a speech and moving the action on. ἐδύσετο is the aorist middle of δύω ‘put on’, with ἀμφ’ ὤμοισιν ‘around the shoulders’. τεύχεα καλά is ‘fine armour’. ὦρσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’ (the active of ὦρτο above), and the three men are the three named at 297. ἄνωγεν is the third singular of ἄνωγα, a perfect with present sense (‘I command’), used here as a narrative past, ‘bade’; ἔντε’ ἀρήϊα is ‘warlike gear’ (ἔντεα, arms and equipment) and ἑλέσθαι the aorist infinitive of αἱρέομαι, ‘take’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δέ οἱ οὐκ ἀπίθησαν, ἐθωρήσσοντο δὲ χαλκῷ,
ὤϊξαν δὲ θύρας, ἐκ δ’ ἤϊον·
sentences.l:
And they did not disobey him, and armed themselves with bronze,
and opened the doors, and out they went;
sentences.i: They did not disobey him, but armed themselves with bronze, and opened the doors and went out;
sentences.n: οἱ δέ οἱ: the first οἱ is the pronoun ‘they’ (nominative), the second the dative ‘to him’. ἀπίθησαν is the aorist of ἀπιθέω ‘disobey’. ἐθωρήσσοντο is the imperfect middle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’, ‘armed themselves’, with the dative χαλκῷ ‘with bronze’. ὤϊξαν is the aorist of ἀνοίγνυμι ‘open’, and ἤϊον the epic third plural imperfect of εἶμι, ‘were going’, in tmesis with ἐκ, so ‘out they went’. The sentence ends in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: ἦρχε δ’ Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l: and led Odysseus.
sentences.i: and Odysseus led the way.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of the line, and is one clause. ἦρχε is the imperfect of ἄρχω, ‘led the way’; the same verb meant ‘begin’ in ἤρξατο at 310.

sentences.t:
ἤδη μὲν φάος ἦεν ἐπὶ χθόνα, τοὺς δ’ ἄρ’ Ἀθήνη
νυκτὶ κατακρύψασα θοῶς ἐξῆγε πόληος.
sentences.l:
Already light there was over the earth, but them Athena,
having hidden in night, quickly led out of the city.
sentences.i: It was already light over the earth, but Athena hid them in night and quickly led them out of the city.
sentences.n: ἦεν is the epic imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦν), and φάος the epic ‘light’ (Attic φῶς). ἤδη μὲν … τοὺς δ’ ἄρ’ sets the daylight against what Athena does: ‘already it was light, but them …’. τοὺς is the pronoun ‘them’, the object of ἐξῆγε (imperfect of ἐξάγω). κατακρύψασα is the aorist participle of κατακρύπτω ‘hide’, and νυκτί is the dative ‘in night’. πόληος is the Homeric genitive of πόλις (Attic πόλεως), ‘out of the city’, with ἐξ- of the verb.
